title: One light in two bodies
hookLine: husband and wife are not those who merely sit together, but one light in two bodies (Suhi Var M3, ang 788)
tomorrow: their first real fight. who's supposed to give first?

lines: TWO PEOPLE, TWO SCREENS, ONE COUCH.
ANG 788: NOT THOSE WHO MERELY SIT.
cards: Two people on one couch, each scrolling their own phone, each lit by their own little screen.
That's how Simran finds Jasleen and Aman on Wednesday at his parents' place: four days married, Aman still job hunting, together all day and somehow not.
Then she remembers a line Bebe read at the wedding, from ang 788, and it sounds almost rude. They are not called husband and wife, it says, who merely sit together. Merely sit together?
Sitting together is what married people do.

teach.h: SALOK OF GURU AMAR DAS, ANG 788.
teach.b: Read the whole line and the puzzle opens.

It's a salok of Guru Amar Das in the Var of Raag Suhi, on ang 788, and in paraphrase it says: they are not called husband and wife who merely sit together; they alone are called husband and wife who have one light in two bodies.

teach.h: JOT: THE ONE LIGHT IN EVERY BEING.
teach.b: The word for light is jot, the same light Gurbani sees in every being. So the line isn't against sitting together.
It's saying sitting together isn't the measure. You can share an address, a couch, a last name, and still be two separate lights side by side.

teach.h: TWO BODIES KEPT; ONE LIGHT SHARED.
teach.b: What makes a marriage, in this line, is the same light moving through both of you: the same Name remembered, the same care, the same direction. Here's the surprising part to tell a friend.
The line keeps two bodies. It doesn't ask either person to disappear into the other. Two people, two bodies, two sets of opinions about the thermostat.
One light. Simran doesn't say any of that out loud. She just takes both phones, sets them face down on the coffee table, and asks them what they want for dinner.
Aman answers for Jasleen. He's right.

how: Sikh couples often hear this salok of Guru Amar Das at or around the Anand Karaj, and it is sometimes printed on wedding cards.

games.q: what does “one light in two bodies” mean?
o: two people who have lived together for many years
a couple who agree on absolutely everything
a marriage where one light is shared by two people

games.q: the line, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
p: a salok of Guru Amar Das
not the measure of a marriage
light, the one light in every being

s: the line says husband and wife should become one person
it keeps two bodies; what's shared is one light.
the word for light here, jot, is the light Gurbani sees in every being
the same light, moving through both.
living under one roof makes two people husband and wife in this line
they are not called husband and wife who merely sit together.

games.q: a couple you know never fights and never talks; they share a house and a calendar and little else. going by ang 788, what's missing?
o: the shared light: the same care and direction moving through both.
nothing; living peacefully under one roof is the whole point.
one of them should give up their opinions so they become one.
games.why: Guru Amar Das: not those who merely sit together, but one light in two bodies. two bodies kept; one light shared.

practice: Think of someone you share your days with, a partner, a parent, a roommate, a friend. Choose one small kind thing you could do for them that they won't have to ask for: making the tea, taking the trash out, a note on the counter.
Hold that one act in mind, and the person, through the sit.

wordCard.voice: One light in two bodies. Guru Amar Das's picture of a true marriage: not two people who merely sit together, but one light shared.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jot, light; 'ek jot doe moortee', one light, two forms, on ang 788.

carryVoice: One light, two bodies, and still two very different opinions about the thermostat. That's today.

sources.ref: Ang 788 (Suhi ki Var, salok of Guru Amar Das: dhan pir eh na aakhian behan ikathe hoe, ek jot doe moortee dhan pir kaheeai soe), paraphrased
